I have farmed these 9 mu in Quzhou for 40 years, and I know every corner of my land. The wheat-maize double crop is my family's bread and butter — it is reliable and the grain buyers come right to the village — so I will put 6 mu into that rotation. I sow wheat in mid-October after the National Day rush, and when we cut it in early June there is barely a week before the maize must go in, so I plant the maize no-till straight into the wheat stubble. For the wheat, I rotary till the field first, then spread about one bag of compound fertilizer and half a bag of urea per mu before planting; at green-up I topdress another half bag of urea if the leaves look pale. Because I have my own tube well, I will water the wheat four times: once in winter so the cold does not kill it, and three times in spring when the north wind dries everything out.

I keep 2 mu of cotton because Lao Zhang down the road gets good money for it, and I have grown cotton long enough to know the routine. But I am 58 now and my knees ache, so I cannot expand it — picking cotton and spraying for bollworm every week is hard work. I buy the improved seed 99-1 from the township market. I will rotary till that plot in April, give it some compound fertilizer at planting, and irrigate twice when the flowers open and the bolls are swelling. I figure about 12 sprays this summer to keep the worms off.

The last 1 mu I plant with mungbean. We eat mungbean porridge in winter, and any extra sells at the village fair. I keep my own seed from last year, and because mungbean puts nitrogen into the soil I do not buy fertilizer for it. I will till it with the rotary tiller, water it once if July is scorching, and spray twice for pod borer. My sons work in Shijiazhuang now, so for wheat harvest and cotton picking I will hire a few days of labor, but my husband and I can manage the rest.
